newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Euro-MPs to demand clampdown on "sex tourism".
newsitem.headline: Euro-MPs to demand clampdown on "sex tourism".

text.p: In the wake of the child sex abuse scandals which rocked Belgium this summer, the European Parliament is due on October 24 to demand urgent European Union action to combat sex tourism.

"Anybody who goes abroad to indulge in child sex abuse should be prosecuted," Irish Christian Democrat Mary Banotti, a leading campaigner to prevent the sexual exploitation of children, told Reuters on Tuesday.

Since July, Euro-MPs have been calling for action on all fronts to stamp out child sex abuse, from police cooperation on trafficking in human beings to preventing paedophiles spreading pornography on the Internet.
Now Euro-MPs are expected to ask the EU to include special measures to stamp out sex tourism in its 1997-2000 programme to promote the European tourist industry.

While they are expected to approve the new programme - COM(96)168 - on October 24, Euro-MPs will insist it go further than its declared aims of improving the quality of Europe's tourism industry, boosting jobs in the sector and protecting the environment.
The European Commission is due to publish a discussion paper on sex tourism before the end of the year but Euro-MPs think it should start thinking about concrete action now.

In a report drafted by Spanish Christian Democrat Francisca Bennasar Tous, the parliament will demand that the so-called Philoxenia programme fund a study of the geographic, economic, legal and cultural factors which encourage sex tourism.

Euro-MPs will say this analysis should form the basis of a well-targeted strategy to fight the dark underside of the tourist industry - child rape, prostitution, trafficking in human beings, pornography and its distribution through the Internet.
Bannotti believes Europeans have turned a blind eye to the problem for so long because it mainly concerns European tourists going to third countries like Thailand.
"We've been far too lax. As long as it's been far away we have been able to avoid it," she said.
But European cities like Amsterdam have their fair share of sex tourists too and European travel agents are implicated in the sordid trade.
Bannotti said she wanted travel agents offering sex tours to be prosecuted too.

The chairman of parliament's tourism committee, Dutch Christian Democrat Petrus Cornelissen, is to meet European tour operators on November 4 to discuss parliament's suggestion for a code of conduct for the industry outlawing unsavoury and dangerous practices.
Euro-MPs will also be urging the European Commission to use funds from the Philoxenia programme for an EU-wide advertising campaign condemning sex tourism.

Bannotti believes this could be backed up by another kind of publicity campaign: "I have great belief in the power of embarrassment to change things. If people had their names published in the papers back home, they might think twice about going abroad for child abuse," she said.
As Bennasar Tous's report points out, tourism is the most important economic activity in the world.
The United Nations said it will generate more income in 2000 than the steel, automobile or oil industries.
But although Europe is still the world's major tourist destination, its leadership is being increasingly challenged.
Bennasar Tous believes Europe needs to start catering more accurately for specific categories of tourist such as the elderly, the young, the handicapped and so on.

The industry could do itself a big favour by clamping down on sub-standard tourist accommodation, says Bannotti, who has been campaigning on behalf of the sons of an Irish couple who died of carbon monoxide poisoning in a Tenerife holiday complex.
"We need proper safety standards in tourist accommodation. We need to look at the availability of health care for people who get ill or are injured on holiday.
"And above all we need a tourism ombudsman so people can go to a one-stop shop. At the moment it is almost impossible for ordinary people to follow through a complaint," Bannotti explained.
